facts.text: A terrain model describes ground shape; a digital elevation model (DEM) is its simplest form, a mesh is a surface of small triangles rendered by a computer, and a collision proxy is an invisible simplified shape used to detect contact.
facts.quote: A terrain model describes the shape of the ground, a digital elevation model (DEM) is its simplest form, a mesh is the surface of small triangles that a computer draws, and a collision proxy is the invisible simplified shape used to detect contact.

facts.text: A digital elevation model is a grid of ground heights, and a mesh converts that grid or a scanned object into connected triangles that a graphics card can render.
facts.quote: A mesh turns that grid, or any scanned object, into a surface of connected triangles that a graphics card can render

facts.text: One quarry pit model in the booklet was optimized to 50,000 polygons, meaning 50,000 triangles.
facts.quote: one quarry pit model in the booklet was "optimized to 50,000 polygons", that is, 50,000 triangles [Chapter 5]

facts.text: The booklet also uses DEM to mean the discrete element method, a soil-physics technique unrelated to digital elevation grids; context distinguishes the two meanings.
facts.quote: the booklet also uses DEM for the discrete element method, a soil-physics technique that has nothing to do with elevation grids; context tells them apart.

facts.text: Detailed meshes are slow to test for contact, so simulators use simpler invisible collision proxies, such as boxes or smoothed surfaces, for physics-engine contact detection with berms or workers.
facts.quote: Detailed meshes are slow to test for contact, so simulators attach a collision proxy: a simpler invisible shape (a box, a smoothed surface) that the physics engine uses to decide whether the machine touched the berm or the worker.

facts.text: Scenes reconstructed from photographs by neural methods have no native collision surface.
facts.quote: Scenes built from photographs by neural methods have no native collision surface

facts.text: One pipeline cited in the booklet required invisible collision substrates beneath Gaussian Splatting.
facts.quote: one cited pipeline needed "invisible collision substrates beneath the Gaussian Splatting" [Chapter 5]

facts.text: A mesh that misplaces a berm edge by tens of centimeters can corrupt a stopping-distance test.
facts.quote: A mesh that places a berm edge tens of centimeters from its true position can corrupt a stopping-distance test [Chapter 5].

facts.text: For braking, ground friction, sinkage, cohesion and moisture affect how a machine stops and pitches; pitching changes sensor position. These mechanical terrain effects fall under terramechanics.
facts.quote: Friction, sinkage, cohesion and moisture change how the machine stops and how it pitches, which moves the sensors. That is the terrain model in the physics sense, covered under terramechanics.

facts.text: The booklet found no validation of simulated braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes for heavy machines, leaving the ground layer of every virtual site a known gap rather than a solved problem.
facts.quote: The booklet found no validation of simulated braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes for heavy machines, so the ground layer of every virtual site is a known gap, not a solved problem [Chapter 5].
